source.title: National curriculum in England: geography programmes of study

coverage.note: Structured controlled paraphrases of the statutory programme of study. Example content shown in square brackets in the source is not treated as a statutory requirement.

KS1.summary: Name and locate the seven continents and five oceans.
Name, locate and identify characteristics of the four countries and capital cities of the United Kingdom and its surrounding seas.
Compare human and physical geography of a small area of the United Kingdom with a contrasting small area in a non-European country.
Identify seasonal and daily weather patterns in the United Kingdom and locate hot and cold areas in relation to the Equator and the North and South Poles.
Use basic geographical vocabulary for key physical features such as coasts, rivers, mountains, soil, vegetation, seasons and weather.
Use basic geographical vocabulary for key human features such as cities, towns, villages, farms, ports, harbours and shops.
Use world maps, atlases and globes to identify the United Kingdom, its countries, and studied countries, continents and oceans.
Use simple compass directions and locational or directional language to describe features and routes on maps.
Use aerial photographs and plan perspectives to recognise landmarks and basic human and physical features, devise simple maps, and use or construct basic symbols and keys.
Use simple fieldwork and observation to study the geography of the school, its grounds and the surrounding environment.

KS2.summary: Locate countries with a focus on Europe, including Russia, and North and South America, considering environmental regions, key physical and human characteristics, countries and major cities.

Name and locate UK counties, cities and geographical regions, including their human and physical characteristics, topographical features and land-use patterns, and understand how some have changed over time.
Identify the position and significance of latitude, longitude, the Equator, hemispheres, the Tropics, polar circles, the Prime or Greenwich Meridian and time zones.
Compare human and physical geography of a UK region, a region in a European country and a region in North or South America.
Describe and understand key aspects of physical geography including climate zones, biomes, vegetation belts, rivers, mountains, volcanoes, earthquakes and the water cycle.

Describe and understand key aspects of human geography including settlement, land use, economic activity and trade links, and the distribution of natural resources such as energy, food, minerals and water.
Use maps, atlases, globes and digital or computer mapping to locate countries and describe studied features.
Use eight-point compass directions, four- and six-figure grid references, symbols and keys, including Ordnance Survey maps, to develop knowledge of the United Kingdom and wider world.
Use fieldwork to observe, measure, record and present local human and physical features using methods such as sketch maps, plans, graphs and digital technologies.

KS3.summary: Extend locational knowledge and spatial awareness by studying Africa, Russia, Asia including China and India, and the Middle East, including environmental regions, key physical and human characteristics, countries and major cities.
Understand geographical similarities, differences and links through study of a region in Africa and a region in Asia.

Understand physical geography processes including geological timescales, plate tectonics, rocks, weathering, soils, weather and climate change from the Ice Age to the present, glaciation, hydrology and coasts.
Understand human geography processes including population and urbanisation, international development, economic sectors from primary to quaternary, and natural-resource use.
Understand how human and physical processes interact to influence and change landscapes, environments and climate, and how human activity depends on functioning natural systems.
Build and routinely apply knowledge of globes, maps and atlases in classroom and field settings.
Interpret Ordnance Survey maps using grid references and scale, topographical and thematic mapping, and aerial and satellite photographs.
Use Geographical Information Systems (GIS) to view, analyse and interpret places and data.
Use fieldwork in contrasting locations to collect, analyse and draw conclusions from geographical data using multiple increasingly complex sources.
